topic.angle: Thesis estimates and the Sydney Opera House

card.title: The thesis that took 22 days longer

panels.text: In a 1994 study, 37 psychology students estimated how long their senior thesis would take. The average guess: 33.9 days.
They also guessed the best case, 27.4 days, and the worst case, 48.6 days.
The average actual time was 55.5 days, longer than even the worst-case guess. Only about 30% finished in the time they predicted.
That is the planning fallacy: optimistic time predictions, even when similar tasks have run long before. Outside observers tend to overestimate the time instead.
Sydney Opera House was expected in 1963. A scaled-down version opened in 1973, at $102 million against an original estimate of $7 million.

probes.question: In the 1994 study, what was the students' average actual completion time?
True or false: outside observers predicting someone else's task time tend to be optimistic.

claims.claim: Average actual time 55.5 days (probe 1) and about 30% finished in the predicted time
claims.quote: The average actual completion time was 55.5 days, with about 30% of the students completing their thesis in the amount of time they predicted.

claims.claim: Title '22 days longer' and 'longer than even the worst-case guess'
claims.note: Verified by calculation: 55.5 - 33.9 = 21.6, which rounds to 22 days; 55.5 > 48.6.

claims.claim: Optimistic predictions even when similar tasks have run long before
claims.quote: regardless of the individual's knowledge that past tasks of a similar nature have taken longer to complete than generally planned

claims.claim: Outside observers tend to overestimate the time, i.e. are not optimistic (probe 2)
claims.quote: when outside observers predict task completion times, they tend to exhibit a pessimistic bias, overestimating the time needed
